speaker: Will Guidara
title: Talking Unreasonable Hospitality, Culture, and Leadership with Will Guidara
question: In hospitality and retail turnarounds, why does aggressively selling a new vision right after taking over a team often backfire?
guest: I think when you're trying to usher a culture through transition, the last thing you should do as a leader is sell your team on an idea. Because if you're a good salesperson, you can get someone to buy something they don't want. And they're going to wake up a few months later and say, "Gosh, what am I doing? This is not what I want." Rather, I got there and did nothing for three months, outside of just talking to the people on my team. I've learned since that at Chanel, there's a rule when a new executive joins the team: they are not allowed to talk in a manager meeting for three months. So many people feel like when they join a new organization, they need to prove their worth as quickly as possible, when the best thing they can do is just shut up and listen for a while.

points.core: Persuasive leaders can talk employees into agreeing to changes they secretly oppose.
points.note: Accept: strong salesmanship induces superficial buy-in from staff who do not genuinely want the new direction. Do not credit: generic advice to communicate clearly or be transparent.

points.core: Staff talked into an unwanted vision eventually disengage months into the transition.
points.note: Accept: oversold employees experience delayed realization of mismatch, resentment, or attrition months later. Do not credit: vague claims that organizational change is hard or causes immediate pushback.

points.core: Rushing to prove authority early blocks new leaders from diagnosing team realities.
points.note: Accept: spending the first months listening silently before acting is required to understand existing dynamics before leading change. Do not credit: generic platitudes about building rapport or showing humility.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
It backfires because a new leader has authority but not yet credibility, and a vision pitch asks for trust before any has been earned.

Frontline staff in struggling hotels, restaurants and stores have usually lived through several managers and "fresh starts" already. A bold vision on day one sounds like the last one that went nowhere, so it triggers cynicism rather than energy. It also carries an implied insult: declaring what must change before you have listened suggests that the people there are the problem and that their knowledge of the customers, the building and the workarounds doesn't matter.

There is a practical problem too. The leader doesn't yet know why things are broken, so the vision is often wrong in its details, and staff spot that immediately. Meanwhile, the daily irritants they care about—broken equipment, chaotic rosters, understaffing, unfair policies—remain unfixed, making the talk look detached from reality.

The result is quiet compliance, passive resistance or turnover among the experienced people you most need.

What tends to work is the reverse order: listen, fix a few visible pain points quickly, then build the vision with the team's input.

The response mentions resistance and turnover without linking them to employees realizing months later that they accepted a vision they never wanted.
The response links pitching a vision prematurely to an incomplete diagnosis of operational problems and puts listening before setting the direction.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: In hospitality and retail turnarounds, frontline teams are typically exhausted by daily operational friction—short staffing, broken equipment, erratic schedules, and frustrated customers—and jaded by past leadership initiatives that went nowhere. Aggressively pitching a grand vision before listening signals that the new leader is disconnected from floor reality, triggering immediate cynicism and change fatigue. Worse, sweeping talk of transformation implicitly devalues the staff's past efforts, breeding defensiveness among the people who kept the business running under tough conditions. Because guest and shopper experiences depend directly on frontline morale and discretionary effort, alienating the floor quickly hurts service quality and staff retention. Layering strategic demands onto unstable operations also creates confusion when employees lack the basic tools, training, and coverage to execute core routines. Effective turnaround leaders earn credibility first by observing shifts, listening to frustrations, and fixing tangible daily bottlenecks, ensuring that when a broader vision is introduced, the team trusts both the leader and their own capacity to deliver it.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Pushing a new vision hard in the first weeks usually backfires because the new leader hasn't earned the credibility to make the case yet. Frontline staff in hotels, restaurants and stores have often lived through several "transformations" and several managers. To them, a polished pitch sounds like one more corporate rollout that will fade, so they nod along and wait it out. A big vision also suggests that the way they've been working was wrong. That can insult people who kept things running through understaffing and bad systems, and it pushes them toward defending how things are done now.

There's a practical problem too. A newcomer doesn't yet know why things work the way they do, such as informal workarounds, key regulars, supplier quirks or which employees others actually follow. A vision built before learning those can be naive, and staff notice right away.

What tends to work better is to listen first, fix a few visible frustrations quickly (broken equipment, scheduling problems) and stay present on the floor. Then build the vision with the team, using what they've told you. Small early wins show you'll follow through, and staff are more likely to back a plan they helped shape.

points.why: Staff nod along because they already expect the rollout to fade, so their apparent agreement comes from skepticism rather than persuasion.
The response describes staff deciding from the outset to wait out the rollout and omits any delayed realization or disengagement after being persuaded.
The response explains how moving too early leaves the vision uninformed by frontline realities that the leader needs to learn by listening.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
In hospitality and retail turnarounds, frontline teams are typically exhausted, cynical, and accustomed to high leadership turnover. When a new leader immediately pushes a grand vision, it often feels like another disconnected corporate slogan rather than genuine leadership. Staff in struggling stores, restaurants, or hotels already face daily operational pain points—broken equipment, chaotic scheduling, stockouts, or chronic understaffing—and hearing lofty promises while those basics remain unaddressed quickly destroys credibility.

Aggressively selling change also triggers defensiveness. It implicitly dismisses the team’s past effort and local knowledge, alienating the experienced employees whose buy-in directly shapes the guest experience. Because hospitality and retail depend on real-time service execution, reluctant staff can easily undermine a new direction through quiet disengagement.

In these environments, trust is built backward: leaders earn the right to cast a vision by first listening, working alongside the team, and fixing immediate friction points. Once employees see practical relief and competence, they become far more receptive to a bigger future.

points.why: The response describes defensiveness and alienation but never says persuasive selling can secure apparent agreement from employees who oppose the vision.
The response mentions quiet disengagement but never connects it to employees realizing months later that they were talked into a direction they did not want.
The response presents listening as a way to earn trust without explaining how rushing to prove oneself prevents a new leader from understanding the team's existing dynamics.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A new leader is asking for trust before the team has seen how they lead. In hospitality and retail, frontline staff know where service breaks down and which past initiatives fizzled. If the leader immediately pushes a new vision without listening, staff may hear an implicit criticism of their work or another promise from someone who doesn’t understand the day-to-day reality. They may nod along while withholding the candid feedback the turnaround depends on.

Listening across shifts, following through on commitments, and fixing a problem staff deal with every day give the team a reason to believe the leader. The vision then has a concrete connection to their work and a track record behind it.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Right after a takeover, the new leader has a vision, but the team has experience the leader still needs. Frontline staff know why the checkout line backs up or rooms are late for check-in. Some have also watched earlier turnaround promises go unfulfilled. Selling a plan before hearing them can sound like a verdict on their work, especially if the plan overlooks problems they face every shift. People may nod along while keeping their doubts and ideas to themselves. The leader can then mistake silence for support.

A better start is to explain the direction, work alongside the team, and follow through on a problem they identify. That gives staff a concrete reason to trust the leader’s judgment and a chance to shape how the vision will work in practice.
